newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - FITIC HITS THE SPOT.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - FITIC HITS THE SPOT.

text.p: Buoyed by a wave of China fever, Fujian International Trust and Investment Corp (FITIC) launched its own US$100 million 144a overnight Thursday.
"Hutchison helped generate (China) euphoria," said one banker involved in the deal, referring to the successful US$2 billion global from Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.
The deal was priced to float at 123 basis points over the underlying treasuries, against 82 basis points for Hutchison, also a 10-year issue.
"If you're looking at Asia as a region, you're only going to be able to do deals in Hong Kong and China (credits)," one banker commented.
In other news, Societe Generale Asia has produced an innovative structure in which a floating-rate note issue in U.S. dollars is backed by a convertible loan in Hong Kong dollars.
Some HK$1.46 billion in convertible loans notes will be issued by Hongkong China Ltd to Lippo Ltd.

Of this, HK$890 million will be taken up by a "bankruptcy remote" special purpose vehicle (SPV) incorporated in the Cayman Islands, which will issue US$100 million in FRNs to finance the purchase of the convertible notes.
The notes mature in two years, and are convertible into shares in Hongkong China at HK$5.617 a share.
Bankers said the U.S. dollar equivalent of the nominal amount of the convertible notes bought by the SPV would be not less than 115 percent of the issue amount of the FRNs.

The SPV will also enter into a Hong Kong dollar/U.S. dollar cross-currency swap with Lippo through which the one percent coupon that the SPV gets from its convertible notes will be swapped into 1.5 percentage points over the London Interbank Offered Rate to service the FRN interest payments.
This leaves the FRN with no exposure.

Hongkong China can redeem the convertible notes at any time before maturity, and Lippo can also repurchase the convertible notes from the SPV every six months after the second interest payment on the FRNs.
If either of these happens, the FRNs will be redeemed at the same time, bankers said.
Despite the relatively complicated structure, bankers expected it to go well.
"It's good pricing -- it'll go well," said one observer. "Hongkong China hasn't borrowed in its own name."

"Hongkong China is a rare asset (in the debt market)," he said, adding that investors would like the purpose of the deal -- acquiring a 50 percent stake in a financial services company in which the other 50 percent shareholder was a China red chip.
